issues.legal_issue: The Supreme Court may admit material additional evidence in an appeal under its inherent power when the evidence could not have been produced before the decision under appeal and its consideration is necessary for justice.
material_facts: The plaintiffs appealed after the High Court dismissed their mortgage suit for failure to prove due attestation of the will under which they claimed the mortgage rights.
Probate of the will was granted after the High Court’s decision, so it could not have been produced there.
The plaintiffs applied in the Supreme Court appeal to place the probate on the record as additional evidence.
issues.conclusion: The Supreme Court had power to admit additional evidence and admitted the probate for consideration in deciding the appeal.
issues.legal_principle: Rule 5 of Order 45 of the Supreme Court Rules recognises the Court’s inherent power to make orders necessary for the ends of justice or to prevent abuse of process. The Court’s power to admit additional evidence is no less than that of the Privy Council, as stated in Inderjit Pratap Sahi v. Amar Singh. In Lachmeshwar Prasad Shukul v. Keshwar Lal Chaudhuri, the Federal Court affirmed that an appellate court may consider changes in fact or law occurring after the decision under appeal when justice requires.

predicates.appeal_proceeding: The matter is being considered in an appeal.
predicates.material_evidence_arose_after_lower_deci: Material evidence came into existence after the decision under appeal and therefore could not have been produced before that decision.
predicates.evidence_is_necessary_for_justice: Considering the evidence is necessary to determine the appeal justly.

issues.definition: When an appeal involves material evidence that arose only after the lower decision and is necessary for justice, the evidence may be admitted.

issues.legal_issue: A probate judgment obtained after the decision under appeal must be considered as a judgment in rem, and its effect is not defeated because the opposing parties were not parties to the probate proceedings.
material_facts: Probate of the will was granted after the High Court dismissed the suit for failure to prove the will’s attestation.
The probate was granted in favour of the plaintiffs and another beneficiary and was placed before the Supreme Court in the appeal.
The opposing parties objected that they had not been parties to the probate proceedings.
The probate addressed the deficiency in proof of attestation on which the High Court had based its decision.
issues.conclusion: The probate had to be taken into consideration in deciding the appeal; the objection based on the opposing parties’ absence from the probate proceedings was unsustainable, and the attestation-related infirmity in the plaintiffs’ case was removed.
issues.legal_principle: A probate judgment is a judgment in rem, so its effect is not avoided merely because an opposing party was not a party to the probate proceedings. An appellate court may take account of supervening facts when deciding an appeal, as recognised in Lachmeshwar Prasad Shukul v. Keshwar Lal Chaudhuri, following the principle stated in Patterson v. State of Alabama. The grant of probate removed the infirmity arising from the failure to prove due attestation under section 63(1)(c) of the Indian Succession Act.

predicates.appeal_proceeding: The matter is being decided in an appeal.
predicates.probate_granted_after_lower_decision: A court granted probate after the decision under appeal.
predicates.probate_is_judgment_in_rem: The probate determination is a judgment that operates in rem.

issues.definition: In an appeal, a probate judgment granted after the lower decision must be considered despite an objection that the objecting party did not participate in the probate proceedings.
